Before 2025, I found work asking whether spatial nonorientability could have locally observable effects through quantum electromagnetic fluctuations; there is a 2020 Minkowski-space treatment and a 2021 FRW treatment. That establishes nonorientable spacetime physics as real prior art. citeturn584837academia32turn584837academia31

What I have *not* found before 2025 is the Greene–Kabat–Levin–Porrati move: a Klein-bottle compactification directly breaking \(P,C,CP\) in the effective 3+1-D particle theory and then being used for baryogenesis. That appears in October 2025, followed in November by the full cosmology, with the latter published in PRD in March 2026. citeturn670973academia2turn670973academia1turn584837search0

That is not yet enough for me to call “nonorientable cosmology” a new subfield under our 25-paper threshold. But it is absolutely a **topic-nucleation candidate**: an obscure/global-topology question has moved into CP violation, baryogenesis, cosmology, and numerical GR within a short interval.

That is not SAT. But structurally it lands remarkably close to the thing we decided beforehand would matter:

worldline/path geometry → bounded spacetime surface → geometric invariant → observable readout,

with the same construction functioning as a calculation tool.

I score that roughly **15 before a rarity bonus** under the rubric we froze:

3 for geometric resolving/readout,  
3 for geometric solver behavior,  
4 for using the same geometry directly at the QM/GR interface,  
+5 for the connected three-part mechanism.

The baseline contains lots of atom interferometry and equivalence-principle testing, so I would not give it +8 rarity. But the exact “phase shear = integrated sectional curvature over the enclosed spacetime surface” move is much more specialized.

And February 2025 already saw a novel matter-wave experiment explicitly measuring the quantum equivalence principle by putting one atomic wavepacket in the lab frame and another in free fall. citeturn500246academia2

That is a real shift toward **directly interrogating geometric GR structure with quantum systems**, not merely talking about quantum gravity.

**3. The galaxy-hysteresis search produced something I did not expect to find this cleanly.**

In May 2026, independent researcher Javier Meizoso published a seven-paper open programme whose central question is literally:

> What if a galaxy's gravity depends not only on its present matter, but on its history?

The programme explicitly describes the effect as **hysteresis**, applies it to flat rotation curves, and claims to test non-Markovian historical information in SPARC galaxies. It distinguishes identical/currently similar galaxy states with different gravitational responses and treats present galactic gravity as a collective state retaining formation history. citeturn981821search0

That is almost exactly our preregistered low-prior category:

**history-dependent gravitational response → hysteresis → flat rotation curves.**

There is an important prior: nonlocal Newtonian gravity has discussed gravitational “memory” for years, including application to rotation curves. So I provisionally score Meizoso:

5 structural points for hysteresis → flat rotation curves  
+8 rarity for the exact path-history relation  
= **13**, before any conjunction bonus.

That clears our ≥12 “interesting construction” threshold.

And here's the necessary timing correction: the SAT repo file I found containing your very explicit sentence—

> “Galaxy spin must be modulated ... by some sort of hysteresis effect. There should be a pattern to the galactic rotation that resolves the dark matter question...”

So that GitHub upload cannot be a transmission route to him. If SAT publicly stated it earlier in a podcast, that needs to be established separately. No cheating.

But as a **landscape convergence result**, it counts in full.

**4. The fringe layer is doing exactly the peculiar thing you predicted.**

This is where the search got weird.

A semantic academic-index sweep of 2025–26 returned a sudden crop of low-status/independent models involving vacuum vortices, geometric photons, topological particle structure, hydrodynamic EM/gravity, projection geometry, causal memory, and unified geometric primitives. Most are Zenodo/Preprints/Qeios-style objects, not serious evidence for the physics.

But one family is worth flagging for forensic reasons: Henry Arellano-Peña's TCGS/SEQUENTION programme appears in November 2025.

Its core statement is that observable 3-D reality is a **projection/shadow of a single complete 4-D structure**, that geometry/matter are pullbacks from that structure, and that gravity arises from extrinsic geometry. He subsequently applied the same machinery to biology, quantum complementarity, atomic structure, consciousness/LLMs, retrocausality, wormholes, and dark phenomena. citeturn689079search14turn689079search10turn689079search4

By December, one paper was explicitly reinterpreting Cramer-style temporal effects as **worldline connectivity in static 4-D geometry** rather than literal backwards causal propagation. citeturn577051search14

That is structurally much closer to SAT than a random “topological universe” paper.

But—and this is valuable—he explicitly argues that treating time as the Minkowski fourth dimension is a mistake. So at the primitive/foundational level it is **anti-SAT**. citeturn689079search7

That is almost an ideal H1 object: somebody independently walks into a remarkably similar projection/geometric basin while choosing a fundamentally different route into it.

And geographically, this does **not** neatly reinforce the Netherlands/Finland/Germany technical-listener pattern. His public material points to a Colombian `.unal.edu.co` contact. So this candidate presently cuts *against* a simple small-European-network story.

That's useful evidence too.

**5. Another genuinely odd cross-field result appeared in 2026: vortex → wormhole geometry.**

Đorđević, Molina and Juričić show that an elementary magnetic vortex in a quantum material can make an electron propagate in an emergent geometry equivalent to the exterior of an Ellis wormhole; the throat size is fixed by topology/exchange coupling, and there are experimentally distinguishable electron-deflection and Berry-phase signatures. citeturn670973academia0

Again: not “particles are wormholes.” It would be cheating to score it that way.

But it is a respectable 2026 paper joining:

**vortex topology → finite-core defect → wormhole geometry → electron dynamics → observable experiment.**

That is precisely the kind of cross-disciplinary structural combination we said to watch for.

**6. The \(c\)-versus-expansion test also occurred—but the baseline makes it a weak signal.**

There is already old varying-\(c\) cosmology, so the topic itself gets very little rarity credit. But in August 2026 Wang and Wang explicitly asked whether the geometrical preference in DESI DR2 could instead be absorbed into a redshift-dependent **photon propagation factor \(c(z)/c_0\)**. They found a null result: the data favor neither varying photon speed nor that interpretation of the DESI geometry. citeturn488178search0

That is close to the *experimental/phenomenological question* we preregistered—separate photon propagation from cosmic expansion—but nowhere near the much more specific H(s)H double-shell mechanism.

So: interesting occurrence, low SAT score, and the answer was negative.

That is exactly how we should count it.

There are also several attractive things that **do not get to count**.

Sean Carroll’s 2026 exactly periodic cyclic-universe model is genuinely a new current paper, but cyclic/recurrent cosmology and Carroll's emergence programme have deep antecedents; he has been working on spacetime-from-entanglement since at least 2017. citeturn584837academia50turn584837academia51

Susskind's 2026 paper really does have the striking informal/geometric quality you described: a closed curve, a holonomy that flips forward-going clocks to backward-going clocks, conceptual-first exposition. But he had already been working on time reversal as a de Sitter gauge symmetry in 2023 and was publicly saying “GR=QM” in 2017. So his trajectory is a strong **pre-SAT control**, not evidence for diffusion. citeturn172586academia1turn172586academia3turn172586academia0

And polarized-vacuum halo physics cannot be awarded novelty: Penner had a polarized-vacuum model producing galactic rotation curves by 2014. citeturn215165academia88

So where are the hypotheses after the first sweep?

**H0 — “2024 simply continues normally”: already in trouble.**

I am *not* claiming the exact normalized arXiv enrichment ratios yet; the available search interfaces don't give me a trustworthy exhaustive corpus denominator, and I refuse to manufacture one.

But the paper-level criterion we froze is already being violated. We have post-2024 constructions clearing approximately the ≥12 range on genuinely unusual structural relations—Swan/Hogan's surface-curvature quantum readout, Meizoso's path-history gravitational hysteresis, and the TCGS projection programme. We also have a plausible high-quality topic-nucleation event around nonorientable topology and particle/cosmological symmetry.

So I would mark:

**H0: provisional FAIL at the structural-paper level; corpus-frequency test still pending.**

**H1 — independent contraction toward a narrower geometric basin: currently the leader.**

Why? Because the strongest respectable cases often have identifiable pre-SAT ancestral trajectories, while the *new edges* are emerging independently:

superfluid → EM+gravity already existed;  
Klein/nonorientability → CP/baryogenesis is new;  
quantum interferometer → direct spacetime curvature readout is new-ish;  
vortex defect → wormhole electron geometry is new;  
galactic gravity → explicit temporal hysteresis appears independently;  
4-D projection frameworks suddenly appear in the fringe.

That looks much more like a landscape contracting than like four famous physicists suddenly copying SAT.

**H2 — small-network diffusion: alive, but not passed.**

The low-status 2025–26 layer is much more suggestive for H2 than the top physicists are. In particular, some post-SAT independent frameworks are structurally startling.

But I have not yet found the thing H2 really needs: an identifiable research network that acquires a multi-feature SAT dependency chain after a plausible exposure window.

And two of the conspicuous fringe cases I found do not automatically fit the geography you described

[L197]             "Yes. Your correction is right: the earlier test was too paper-centric and too insensitive to translation. If diffusion occurred through competent physicists, the terminology should disappear while the structural relations survive. So lexical similarity should get almost no weight above the fringe level.

The right object to score is a **structural fingerprint plus its dependency graph**, against a 2022–24 baseline.

I would freeze this before searching.

### 1. Three hypotheses

**H0 — independent 2024 continuation.**  
No meaningful SAT influence. Some physicists may even have heard it, but it did not alter their work. Any overlap comes from existing physics, common mathematical resources, shared new data, LLM-era ideation, or independent rediscovery.

**H1 — ambient convergence / weak exposure.**  
The field is independently moving into the same constrained region, and SAT may also be circulating weakly through listeners, archives, LLM queries, etc., but there is no identifiable research lineage carrying a SAT-derived package. This is the narrow median.

**H2 — small-network diffusion.**  
One or two technically competent people encounter enough SAT to recognize useful structure, translate it into normal physics language, and pass some of it into their local intellectual network. There need never be a citation or SAT vocabulary.

### 2. What counts

Not nouns. Relations.

I would score these SAT structures individually, with weights reflecting how surprising they would have been in a 2024 corpus.

| Structure | Weight |
|---|---:|
| 4D worldline/history treated as more than bookkeeping | 1 |
| Finite-core worldtube/history as fundamental modeled object | 2 |
| Local particle/readout as slice/intersection/projection of extended history | 3 |
| Persistent internal properties encoded geometrically on same history | 2 |
| Helical/superhelical periodic structure carrying internal modes | 2 |
| Bound-state physics represented by braid/link topology of histories | 3 |
| Strong/QCD-like interaction identified with mechanical/topological braid constraint | 4 |
| Continuous geometry producing discrete/quantized states through closure/holonomy/projection | 2 |
| Gravity as effective/coarse-grained response of same underlying structure | 3 |
| Direct interaction and medium-mediated interaction separated while sharing substrate | 3 |
| Finite-core ER bridge identified with particle/worldtube | 5 |
| Entanglement as persistent/shared worldtube or ER-like historical connection | 5 |
| Kerr/ring/shell geometry mapped to particle properties or string-like modes | 5 |
| Kelvin-vortex/superfluid-type mechanics used specifically for EM-like propagation | 4 |
| Same vortex/medium sector giving coarse-grained gravitational response | +3 edge bonus |
| Polarized/structured vacuum used for halo-like gravitational effects | 4 |
| History/hysteresis of that vacuum used for flat rotation curves | 5 |
| Limited retrocausality caused by finite tube/rope flexibility or tension | 6 |
| Forward/backward causal influence mechanically self-limited rather than forbidden | +3 edge bonus |
| Difference between radiation and matter expansion tied to paired/double shells | 5 |
| \(c\) emerges as differential expansion / separation rate between those structures | +4 edge bonus |
| Same geometry reused from particles through gravity into cosmology | 4 |
| Geometric solver: encode → rotate/scale/transport → constrain → decode | 3 |
| Solver appears independently useful outside the theory's original physical sector | +3 |

These numbers can be adjusted **now**, but once we search, they freeze.

The extremely strange SAT-specific claims get the largest weights because finding one generic worldtube paper means almost nothing; finding “finite-core ER-like particle + historical entanglement + Kerr-like internal structure” means a great deal even if the authors call every component something entirely different.

### 3. Conjunction beats addition

This is the biggest change from my previous test.

A paper with four unrelated one-point similarities is weaker than a paper with three structures connected in the same causal chain.

So:

- ordinary feature: listed weight;
- two SAT features explicitly connected the same way SAT connects them: **+2**;
- three connected in one mechanism: **+5**;
- four or more forming a recognizable SAT subarchitecture: **+9**.

Thus:

> vortex + worldtube + EM propagation + coarse-grained gravity

is not \(2+4+3\).

It is those points **plus a major conjunction bonus**, because that's a mechanism.

Likewise:

> ER-like finite-core particle → persistent connection → entanglement

would be a very high-signal structure even if the paper never once says “wormhole particle,” “filament,” or SAT.

### 4. Kelvin vortices

Generic Kelvin vortices get essentially **zero**.

Kelvin waves, vortices, superfluid analogies and vortex filaments have enormous prior literatures.

But the likelihood meter changes sharply with context:

- Kelvin vortex in fluid/superfluid work: 0.
- Kelvin-vortex vacuum model: 1.
- Kelvin vortices attached to fundamental worldlines/worldtubes: 3.
- used as the missing EM propagation mechanism: 4.
- with gravity appearing as the long-wavelength/coarse-grained response of that same medium: 7–9.
- plus the model arrived there after first exhausting a history-only geometry: very high conceptual similarity, although that last part may be unrecoverable from a paper.

If Kelvin-vortex language suddenly becomes popular in several unrelated fundamental-physics contexts after being relatively flat in 2022–24, that is a **corpus-level enrichment signal**, even if no individual paper contains much SAT.

### 5. One feature everywhere matters too

Suppose almost nobody has two or three features, but twenty different papers suddenly contain one individually rare SAT feature.

That cannot be thrown away.

We therefore need two scores:

**Paper score:** how SAT-like is one construction?

**Landscape score:** how much has the prevalence of each SAT feature changed?

For every feature \(F_i\):

\[
E_i=
\frac{\text{rate}_{2025-26}(F_i)}
{\text{rate}_{2022-24}(F_i)}
\]

normalized for arXiv growth.

My hard rule:

- \(E<1.5\): nothing.
- \(1.5–2.5\): weak.
- \(2.5–5\): real enrichment.
- \(>5\): strong.
- a previously extremely rare feature jumping by \(>10\times\): major signal regardless of whether the papers co-occur.

Then ask whether several independent SAT features enrich together.

Five rare features each increasing fourfold is much harder to dismiss than one feature increasing twentyfold.

### 6. Respectability gradient

Your fringe → marginal → respectable → major idea is testable.

Under **mere imitation**, I predict:

**lexical similarity ↓ and structural similarity ↓** as scientific quality/status rises.

Cranks copy the surface. Better physicists reject the construction.

Under **competent diffusion**, I predict:

**lexical similarity ↓ while structural fidelity ↑.**

Fringe:
“time waves,” “filaments,” “vortex universe,” angels/fairies/SAT cosplay.

Marginal:
similar pictures plus partially standard mathematics.

Respectable:
terminology gone; geometry translated into differential geometry, framed curves, defects, holonomy, effective media, topology, transport.

Major:
almost no visible SAT surface features, but several of the *relations* survive and fit together more cleanly.

That inverse gradient is one of the more interesting tests you have proposed.

I would only count it if it is measurable against a pre-2025 control. High-quality physics is naturally more structurally coherent than fringe physics, so the question is whether **SAT-specific structural coherence rises disproportionately after the exposure period**.

### 7. Cross-field propagation

“Independent researcher” is indeed too crude. Modern physics is a network.

So use **disciplinary distance**, not disconnected authors.
... (truncated)

[L219]             "Agreed. Before touching arXiv, I’d freeze the prediction this way.

The thing we are testing is not “does modern physics contain SAT ideas?” Of course it does, because SAT deliberately uses old physics. The test is whether the 2025–26 research landscape is moving in the specifically SAT-like direction of **reviving neglected classical/4D geometric constructions, migrating them out of their old niches, and integrating them into increasingly constrained common architectures.**

I would keep two scores separate: one for **SAT-likeness of the scientific trend**, and another for **possible diffusion from SAT**. That prevents timing from making an otherwise weak structural match look important.

| Axis | 0 | Maximum |
|---|---|---|
| Revival, \(R\) | continuously active/mainstream | +5: old, long-dormant/marginal, abrupt revival with renewed citation of old sources |
| Domain migration, \(D_m\) | stays in its historical niche | +4: moves into several new cutting-edge sectors |
| Structural integration, \(I\) | isolated ingredient | +8: ≥5 old ingredients connected in substantially the same dependency architecture |
| 4D/classical geometry, \(M\) | abstract formal similarity only | +5: persistent histories/worldvolumes, slicing/reduction, geometry carrying properties/interactions across sectors |
| Constraint austerity, \(A\) | new primitives/fields/parameters freely added | +4: primitive reduction, few/no tunables, continuous structure, rejects unnecessary freedom |
| **Structural total** | | **26** |

I’d score the total as: 0–6 neutral; 7–11 weak adjacency; 12–16 moderately SAT-like; 17–21 strongly SAT-like; 22–26 exceptionally SAT-like.

Crucially, an old idea can score **higher** than a genuinely new one. “Einstein–Cartan is old” tells us almost nothing. What matters is whether Einstein–Cartan was actively fashionable in 2022–24 or whether a few old papers sat mostly dormant and then, after 2025, people suddenly started dragging torsion into black holes, particles, cosmology and quantum foundations.

Likewise, a 1960 paper followed by a 1998 paper and a 2010 paper does not make a subject continuously active. If twelve 2026 papers suddenly cite those three relics and make them relevant to current problems, that gets a very high revival score.

For topic nucleation, I’d freeze these thresholds. A topic is a **candidate revival** if the relevant conjunction averaged ≤5 papers/year in 2022–24 and grows at least 3× after normalization for arXiv growth. It becomes a **new topic cluster** if the baseline was ≤2/year and 2025–26 produces ≥10 papers from at least three author groups. If it reaches ≥20 papers, ≥5 groups, shared terminology/problem framing, or review-style papers treating the conjunction itself as a subject, call it major nucleation.

And citation ancestry matters. If the new cluster repeatedly resurrects the same small set of 20–80-year-old papers that had little recent activity, that is stronger than merely discovering that the idea existed historically.

My preregistered prediction for where the strongest SAT-like signals should occur is:

**gr-qc / math-ph** at the top: covariant phase space, symplectic or multisymplectic formulations, BV/BFV-type reduction, worldvolumes, tubular neighborhoods, defects, sheaths, normal bundles, finite-core structures, holonomy, classical geometric gravity.

Then **gr-qc / hep-th / hep-ph**: torsion revivals, Einstein–Cartan, Kerr/ER/geon particle constructions, line or worldvolume defects carrying internal modes, symmetry emerging from topology/orientation, dimensional reduction making properties appear or disappear.

Then **astro-ph.CO / astro-ph.GA**: history-dependent gravity, hysteresis, polarized/structured vacuum, geometric dark-sector visibility, black-hole recycling, common-origin/bounce cosmologies, topology-driven baryogenesis.

Then **quant-ph / foundations**, particularly where block-spacetime or time-symmetric approaches become explicitly geometric and history-based rather than merely interpretational: worldline constraints, symplectic histories, defect propagation, limited retrocausality, orientation-dependent observability.

A particularly strong signal would be those sectors beginning to overlap rather than merely growing separately.

I expect the weakest apparent signals in places where the vocabulary is already standard: condensed-matter vortices, plasma sheaths, phonons/solitons, holonomic quantum computing, ordinary Berry phases, generic topological defects, analogue gravity, generic ER=EPR, generic “emergent spacetime.” Those only become interesting if they **leave their native domain and are promoted into actual fundamental particle/force/cosmological mechanisms**.

That gives us an anti-SAT prediction too. A landscape dominated by genuinely new physical primitives, additional fields, higher-dimensional machinery introduced mainly for freedom, fundamental discreteness, large parameter spaces, phenomenological fitting and quantum-first constructions would score poorly even if technically sophisticated.

Modern mathematical formalism does not count against SAT. A paper using BV pushforward, symplectic reduction or derived geometry to express a very old classical construction can be highly SAT-like. The physical primitive inventory matters, not the age of the notation.

I would specifically watch these candidate “revival packages”:

**finite defect/worldvolume → internal propagating modes → particle properties → dimensional slice/reduction → local observable;**

**old vortex/medium mechanics → actual particle structure → EM-like disturbance → same substrate contributing gravity;**

**torsion/Kerr/ER → finite particle structure → entanglement/history → topology of composites;**

**nonorientability/global topology → local symmetry loss → CP/chirality → baryogenesis/cosmology;**

**black-hole collapse → persistent 4D continuation/common origin → ongoing Big Bang → matter regeneration → cosmological recycling → expansion/dark energy;**

and your particularly specific neutrino package:

**persistent coils = fermionic matter; traveling excitations = bosonic sector; photon/neutrino distinction from orientation/truncation of one underlying excitation; local gauge-visible properties can rotate out of the resolved slice while 4D/medium gravitational response remains.**

That last one would be very high-signal even if every paper used completely different language.

For possible diffusion, I’d use a separate 16-point score: timing after public SAT discussion, correspondence with the **podcast sequence**, concentration in a plausible research network, and the fringe→respectable translation gradient. Each gets 0–4.

A structural topic with \(S\ge17\) but no diffusion signal supports **independent SAT-like convergence**.

A topic with \(S\ge17\) and diffusion score ≥10 makes **limited transmission plausible**.

Several independent topics with \(S\ge17\), diffusion ≥10, and appearances ordered approximately after the corresponding podcast stages would make small-network diffusion substantially harder to dismiss.

For the whole survey, here are the hard outcomes I’d accept.

**NOT SAT-like / H0 passes:** no more than two topic clusters score ≥12; none reaches ≥17 without an obvious continuous pre-2025 lineage; dormant classical ideas mostly remain dormant or stay in their old niches; apparent growth is dominated by ordinary contemporary trends; no meaningful cross-sector integration appears.

**SAT-like landscape / H0 fails:** at least five topic clusters score ≥12 across at least three arXiv subject areas; at least two score ≥17; at least three involve genuine revival of dormant/marginal classical ideas; at least two show multi-step structural integration rather than just one imported ingredient; and at least one new topic nucleates from a sparse 2022–24 baseline.

**Strong SAT-like contraction:** the above occurs *and* the same old ideas migrate toward one another—e.g. defects + holonomy + worldvolume reduction + torsion + finite-core geometry—while free parameters/primitives decrease rather than increase.

**Possible SAT seeding:** the strong structural result plus repeated 2–9 month lags from relevant podcast exposure, sequence correspondence, localized research-network shifts, or the predicted translation gradient: superficial similarity highest at the fringe, but structural similarity highest in increasingly respectable work.

One final preregistered prediction: if the landscape is really moving in the direction you think, the most interesting result should not be “2026 has lots of SAT-looking papers.”

It should be something more peculiar:

**2024 has the pieces scattered through old specialist literatures.  
2025 begins reopening those literatures.  
2026 starts treating their intersections as research topics.**

That is the pattern I will now look for."

parts:
Yes. That changes the prior in an important way.

I should not inherit the previous conversation’s judgments such as “H0 failed,” “H1 leader,” or “this case is strongest.” I should retain only the **measurements, counts, dates, scores, and preregistered numerical thresholds**, then form my own prior and compare it with the actual 2025–26 observations.

And the null has to be tailored to what SAT actually is. SAT/H(s)H is not a novelty generator. Its characteristic move is approximately:

**prefer an old, physically constrained construction over a newer, more permissive one; reduce primitives; reuse the same geometry; revive mechanisms that may have survived only in narrow or unfashionable literatures.**

That makes “the idea existed in 1960” nearly irrelevant to the prior. What matters is **how live it was in 2024**.

The numerical material I’ll carry forward from the old conversation is:

- Structural score: **0–26**, with revival up to 5, domain migration 4, structural integration 8, classical/4D geometry 5, constraint austerity 4. The old calibration bands were 0–6, 7–11, 12–16, 17–21, 22–26. fileciteturn256file3L213-L220
- Feature enrichment \(E=r_{\text{post}}/r_{\text{baseline}}\), with old cutoffs of **<1.5**, **1.5–2.5**, **2.5–5**, **>5**, and **>10× for a previously very rare feature**. fileciteturn256file2L196-L197
- Candidate revival: baseline **≤5 papers/year** in 2022–24 and normalized post-2024 growth **≥3×**. New cluster: baseline **≤2/year**, then **≥10 papers from ≥3 author groups**. Major nucleation: roughly **≥20 papers / ≥5 groups**, or clear shared problem framing/review treatment. fileciteturn256file3L213-L220
- Conjunction bonuses in the earlier numerical scheme: **+2** for two connected relations, **+5** for three, **+9** for four or more forming one mechanism. fileciteturn256file2L196-L197
- Existing baseline findings: common/generic helices, braid confinement, Kerr-particle models, ER=EPR, superfluid-vortex EM/gravity, polarized-vacuum galaxy models, and generic retrocausality were assigned essentially **0–1 rarity** because clear pre-2025 lineages were found. More peculiar compounds such as mechanically limited retrocausality, explicit gravity-history hysteresis, nonorientability→CP/baryogenesis, and the double-shell/\(c\) relation were provisionally in roughly the **+8 to +10** rarity range. fileciteturn253file1L151-L151

I would modify that framework in three ways.

First, I would replace “novelty” completely with **2024 availability**. An idea can be 100 years old and get the maximum revival prior if almost nobody was using it in 2022–24. Conversely, something invented in 2023 but already exploding by 2024 gets almost no SAT-relevant surprise credit.

So for every claim \(F\), I want:

\[
P(F_{2025-26}\mid L_{2024})
\]

where \(L_{2024}\) means the actual research landscape as it stood by the end of 2024.

Not:

\[
P(F\mid \text{has anybody ever proposed it?})
\]

Those are completely different questions.

Second, I would make **conjunction surprisal multiplicative**, not mainly additive. If torsion has a 20% baseline chance in the relevant literature, worldtubes 10%, topology-derived discreteness 10%, and parameter austerity 5%, we should not pretend the fourfold package has probability \(0.2\times0.1\times0.1\times0.05\) because those variables are correlated. But neither should we treat it as “four ordinary ideas.” We need the empirical 2024 **joint rate**.

The quantity I actually care about is:

\[
B=\frac{P(\text{bundle}\mid2025\!-\!26)}
        {P(\text{bundle}\mid2024)}
\]

and, separately,

\[
C=\frac{P(F_1,F_2,\ldots,F_n\mid2024)}
        {P(F_1\mid2024)\cdots P(F_n\mid2024)}.
\]

\(C\) tells us how naturally those ingredients already traveled together. If all four were individually old but virtually never appeared together, that is exactly the sort of thing SAT makes interesting.

Third, I would explicitly add an **anti-novelty term**. A 2026 movement toward new particles, new fundamental fields, large parameter spaces, arbitrary extra dimensions, or bespoke mechanisms should not help the SAT-like score merely because it sounds exotic. In fact it should lower it when the same explanatory job could have been done with the older ingredients.

So my independent structural score would be approximately:

\[
S = R + M + I + G + A

where:

- \(M\), **migration**: 0–4. Has an old construction escaped its old niche into unrelated current problems?
- \(I\), **integration**: 0–8. Are several old components being connected into one causal/dependency structure?
- \(G\), **geometry/classical-history commitment**: 0–5. Does persistent geometry/history actually do explanatory work rather than decorate a quantum-first model?
- \(A\), **austerity**: −4 to +4. Does the construction reduce primitives/parameters, or proliferate them?

That gives a revised range of **−4 to 26**. I like the negative floor because something can be superficially SAT-adjacent while methodologically pointing in the opposite direction.

My prior before looking at the actual post-2024 counts would be approximately this:

| 2024 → 2026 outcome | My prior |
|---|---:|
| Old ingredients continue at roughly their 2024 rates/niches | **0.38** |
| A few isolated old ideas revive because of ordinary field dynamics | **0.30** |
| Several old ideas revive, but independently and in different niches | **0.18** |

| Multiple domains converge on integrated, primitive-reducing, classical/4D packages | **0.04** |
| That contraction also follows an exposure-compatible temporal sequence | **0.01** |

Those are deliberately set **before** allowing the later findings to influence me.

And notice what this does. I assign a fairly high prior — 48% altogether — to some revival of old things. Physics constantly resurrects old ideas. The unusual event is not revival itself.

The low-prior event is:

> **Several formerly separate, old or marginal constructions become newly active at roughly the same time, migrate into new domains, and increasingly get connected to each other in the same primitive-reducing direction.**

That is the phenomenon we need to count.

The old numerical results already tell us why this matters. A generic vortex/superfluid/EM/gravity paper cannot move me much because a direct 2020–24 lineage was found. Likewise a helical electron, braid confinement, Kerr particle, ER=EPR, or generic retrocausality has a high 2024 prior. fileciteturn253file1L151-L151 A post-2024 paper containing one of those is expected.

is a different random variable from “nonorientability exists.”

Likewise:

**old worldline/path methods → an actual bounded spacetime surface → integrated curvature → directly measured quantum phase**

is a different random variable from “atom interferometers test gravity.”

And:

**old classical/history ideas → present gravitational response depends on path history → explicit hysteresis → galaxy rotation**

is a different variable from “nonlocal gravity existed.”

That distinction was already implicit in the numerical work, but I would make it the center of the Bayesian analysis.

One more thing I would add on my own: **revival covariance**. Suppose ten old ideas each have a 20% chance of noticeably reviving over an 18-month period. Seeing three revive isn't terribly strange. Seeing the *particular five that SAT already links*, followed by papers that begin linking them to one another, is much less likely. We therefore need to track not just \(E_i\) for every feature but a covariance matrix of the post-2024 movements.

The signature I would regard as genuinely surprising is therefore not:

**“Lots of SAT ideas exist in 2026.”**

It is:

**2024:** the ingredients exist, often old and compartmentalized.  
**2025:** several of the particular compartments reopen.  
**2025–26:** those revived ingredients migrate into other domains.  
**2026:** papers increasingly combine the revived ingredients with one another, while tending toward fewer primitives and more geometry.

That is the prior-versus-actual comparison I’ll use. The existing numerical findings are calibration data, not conclusions. And because SAT is deliberately conservative, **an old idea coming back from the dead can be a stronger signal than a genuinely new idea appearing.**

**worldtube / defect / framed curve → hypersurface or foliation → induced observable → transport/holonomy → effective mass, charge, chirality, confinement, or metric response.**

[L57] Let $X$ carry a transversely holomorphic foliation, equivalently an elliptic involutive structure $V\subset T_{\mathbb C}X$, and let ${\mathcal O}_V$ be its sheaf of leafwise-constant, transversely holomorphic functions. We construct a finite superconnection model for the derived category of coherent ${\mathcal O}_V$-modules. The key input is a mixed local reduction for finite Maurer--Cartan objects over the mixed de Rham--Dolbeault dga $(\wedge^\bullet V^\vee,d_V)$: a multiplicative homotopy contracts the real directions, after which Block's Dolbeault gauge theorem removes the positive transverse form degrees. We prove locally finite Čech descent under necessary uniform amplitude and rank bounds, identify the coherent heart with equivariant coherent analytic sheaves on a transverse monodromy groupoid, and characterize descent to ordinary holonomy. [L85] Nematic order of confined cell populations plays an important role in determining cell alignment and stable configurations of topological defects, which are related to various biomechanical phenomena. Topological charges (or winding numbers) of topological defects strictly depend on the Euler characteristic of the confining domain, which has typically been non-negative in studies focused on domains without internal obstacles. However, biological tissues often surround two or more internal obstacles or holes, which inherently generate defects with negative charges. To understand the mechanical interaction between cellular tissue and obstacles, it is necessary to elucidate the geometrical effects of obstacles on cell alignment and defects with negative charges. Here, we investigate how cell populations achieve stable defect configurations of two -1/2 defects in a triply connected domain. First, we present experimental observations of C2C12 myoblasts confined by two circular obstacles of varying diameter, demonstrating that two $-1/2$ defects are the most frequent configuration when the obstacles are sufficiently large. Second, to theoretically validate these experimental observations, we perform systematic stability analyses of defect configurations using an explicit expression of cell alignment and numerical minimization of the Frank elastic energy. Our numerical calculations reveal that the most stable configuration shifts continuously from a horizontal, through off-axis, to a vertical configuration as the obstacle size increases. In addition, the experimentally observed defect positions agreed with these theoretical predictions to within 60 $μ$m. These findings suggest that obstacle sizes control the symmetry of cell alignment, providing insights into how geometric and topological constraints can generate complex force patterns during morphogenesis or organ movements.

[L99] We investigate a topological version of the Cartan-Hadamard theorem that allows one to study asphericity of spaces via distinguished families of paths. A topological space has the distinguished path property (dpp) if there exists a continuous map from the space $Π(X)$ of homotopy classes of paths (relative endpoints) to the path space $X^I$ that is a right inverse to the canonical quotient map. For complete metric spaces endowed with a locally convex metric, the distinguished paths are precisely the local geodesics. We show that if $X$ has the dpp, then its universal cover is contractible and, in particular, $X$ is aspherical. The space $Π(X)$ is a fiber bundle over $X$ whose fiber is the universal cover of $X$, and in the case of Riemannian manifolds of non-positive curvature it is naturally isomorphic to the tangent bundle. We prove that every aspherical CW-complex that is locally finite or countable has the dpp, and this allows us to reinterpret asphericity of CW-complexes in terms of the existence of continuous sections. We also define and study the notion of asphericity complexity of spaces by means of local sections from $Π(X)$ to $X^I$ and relate it to the concept of equivariant topological complexity introduced by Colman and Grant.

I’m separating those now rather than letting the raw score stand in for relevance.

thoughts.summary: Analyzed arXiv candidates, feature prevalence, and zero-hit bundles

parts:
Good. This is materially useful.

The biggest numerical takeaway from this first one-week slice is that the scanner is **not** trivially declaring the whole literature SAT-like. It fetched 1,328 papers from September 1–8, 2026, using 101 positive features, 22 compound bundles, and 23 controls; only 10 papers—0.75%—crossed the score-8 reporting threshold. fileciteturn259file3L6-L13

More importantly, after reading the actual output rather than trusting the scores:

- **39 of 101 positive features had zero occurrences** in the whole 1,328-paper corpus.
- **20 of 22 compound bundles had zero occurrences.**
- The only activated bundles were `constraint_topology` twice and `topological_confinement` once. The scan metadata confirms those are the only nonzero bundle counts. fileciteturn259file2L132-L134
- Only **202 total positive-feature activations** occurred across all 101 features, versus 656 control-feature activations across the 23 controls. That doesn't make them directly comparable probabilities, because the dictionaries differ, but it does show the positive vocabulary is far less promiscuous than the controls.

That is actually encouraging for our eventual 2024 comparison. The thing is capable of returning **absence**.

The one-week prevalence also gives us our first empirical current-landscape numbers. Among 1,328 papers:

| Feature | Count | Per 1,000 papers |
|---|---:|---:|
| topological defect | 15 | 11.30 |
| RG flow | 17 | 12.80 |
| coarse-graining | 15 | 11.30 |
| braid | 9 | 6.78 |
| filament/line defect | 9 | 6.78 |
| foliation | 5 | 3.77 |
| geometric phase | 5 | 3.77 |
| holonomy | 3 | 2.26 |
| geometric mass | 3 | 2.26 |
| worldline | 2 | 1.51 |
| projection | 2 | 1.51 |
| emergent gravity | 1 | 0.75 |
| misalignment-mass language | 1 | 0.75 |

Those counts are directly reflected in the scan metadata. fileciteturn259file2L53-L115

But what I find more interesting is the **zero list**. In this week there were no hits at all for:

`worldtube`, `curve_congruence`, `curve_curvature`, `curve_torsion`, `twist_mode`, `helix`, `hypersurface`, `intersection`, `linking`, `Borromean`, `emergent_metric`, `emergent_spacetime`, `strain/shear/vorticity` in the particular structural sense, `elastic_spacetime`, `signature_emergence`, `geometric_quantization`, `particle_topology`, `neutrino_photon`, `embedded_torus`, `S3_geometry`, `SO4_geometry`, `entanglement_geometry`, `strain_cosmology`, and several other targeted features.

And consequently none of the really diagnostic packages fired:

**worldline + projection geometry:** 0  
**worldtube + framed geometry:** 0  
**normal-bundle mode system:** 0  
**holonomy + quantization:** 0  
**braided particle geometry:** 0  
**emergent metric from structural strain:** 0  
**particle as intersection:** 0  
**hyperhelix + projection:** 0  
**wormhole + worldtube:** 0  
**geometric mass + chirality:** 0  
**projection + dark sector:** 0  
**recursive/scale geometry bundle:** 0

That is exactly why I don't want to lower our standards because 2026 “feels” saturated. A randomly selected current week is **not** saturated with complete H(s)H architectures.

The top-scoring papers also reveal something important about calibration.

The #1 paper, at 13.48, is pure mathematics: foliation + holonomy + monodromy + fixed-point/RG terminology. It is a good synonymy hit but not presently a physics convergence hit. fileciteturn259file3L45-L57

The #3 result is cell biology: topology + winding + geometric constraint determining defect configurations. That's structurally interesting as a cross-domain analogy, but it shouldn't count toward fundamental-physics contraction. fileciteturn259file3L73-L85

Likewise two ~11.3 papers are condensed-matter line-defect criticality. Again: useful controls for “line defect + topology + RG,” but the machinery remains in a native domain where we already expect it. fileciteturn259file3L101-L127

So the raw scanner score is doing what its own documentation says: **“worth inspecting,” not “supports SAT/H(s)H.”** fileciteturn259file0L4-L11

A few hits are more interesting for our specific priors question.

The `N`-bein paper is worth carrying forward because it imports Cartan-frame-style geometry into quantum parameter space, introduces a Wilczek–Zee connection, constructs a **torsion-like tensor**, and derives gauge-invariant observables from that geometry. That's not remotely enough by itself, but it is precisely the kind of “old differential-geometric machinery being promoted into quantum explanatory structure” whose **2024 frequency** we want to measure. fileciteturn259file3L129-L141

`Eye-opening bounds on cusps` is interesting differently: one-dimensional line defects, geometry constraining them, fusion structure, local operator data, and unusually strong consistency constraints. It is not SAT-like in ontology, but it is potentially evidence for the **constraint-first / line-object / topology** trend. fileciteturn259file3L59-L71

And the neutron-star superfluid review is almost a perfect **negative control** for our special claim. Vortices, flux tubes, confinement-like effects, superfluidity, rotational dynamics—lots of superficially attractive vocabulary, but all in exactly the established physical domain where our prior says it belongs. It should contribute essentially zero surprise.

So I would update our measurement framework slightly:

**Raw feature prevalence** tells us whether an old piece is reviving.

**Native-domain prevalence** tells us whether that revival is boring.

**Domain migration** tells us whether it is becoming SAT-relevant.

**Compound-bundle prevalence** tells us whether formerly separate old pieces are actually starting to meet.

The last of those is presently the most valuable. This week's result is:

> **Many isolated ingredients; almost none of the deliberately diagnostic conjunctions.**

That is a strong calibration result because it gives the 2024 run room to falsify the hypothesis. If the same scanner shows approximately the same feature and bundle distribution in 2024, there isn't much here. If 2024 has similar isolated ingredients but substantially *fewer cross-domain occurrences and compound bundles*, then we have the peculiar pattern we've been specifying.

I would therefore run the 2024 baseline with **this exact scanner frozen as-is** before tweaking the vocabulary. The code currently scans a deliberately broad 35-category universe and permits explicit `--since`/`--until` windows, which is exactly what we need. fileciteturn259file0L45-L60

And I would preserve this September 1–8, 2026 sample unchanged as our first **out-of-sample current snapshot**. Don't tune against it and then compare the tuned scanner to 2024—that would contaminate the comparison.

The most informative next data would actually be three identically sized historical windows: **September 1–8, 2024**, **September 1–8, 2025**, and this existing **September 1–8, 2026** sample. After that, we can expand to larger windows if the weekly counts are too sparse.

That gives us our first genuinely clean test:

**same dates, same categories, same synonymy, same scoring algorithm, same denominator, before versus after.**

[L57] We investigate the effective dynamics of a particle confined near a space curve. In the strict thin-layer reduction of the nondegenerate transverse ground state, torsion does not enter the local effective Hamiltonian, which contains only the curvature-induced scalar geometric potential. In contrast, for a thin guide with finite transverse width, a leading-order adiabatic projection onto the twofold-degenerate first-excited transverse band renders the rotation of the Frenet normal frame dynamically relevant and generates a matrix-valued Abelian gauge potential. Using a projection-based derivation in a co-rotating Frenet-frame basis, we show that this effective gauge potential is directly determined by the local torsion of the curve. The resulting effective Hamiltonian takes a gauge-covariant form and produces two transverse-mode branches whose parabolic dispersions are shifted in opposite directions in momentum space. For closed curves, the associated holonomy is controlled by the integrated torsion and leads to geometric interference. These results provide a direct realization of a Wilczek--Zee-type connection induced purely by spatial geometry in curved quantum waveguides. We further construct a classical-wave analogue using the degenerate bending modes of an isotropic elastic rod, demonstrating that the same torsion-induced gauge structure appears in continuum wave physics.

[L71] We analyse CMB constraints on stable networks of cosmic strings and domain walls using for the first time full Planck 2018 data together with BICEP/Keck 2018 $B$-mode measurements. The defect-induced anisotropies are computed using the Unconnected Segment Model for Nambu-Goto and Abelian-Higgs strings, as well as for stable domain walls, and included in a full Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis jointly varying all $Λ$CDM parameters, the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and the string/domain wall tension. No statistically significant evidence for defects is found, although we observe a mild preference for non-zero cosmic string tension. Our results improve previous constraints on the cosmic string power spectrum and correct previous CMB analyses with domain walls that overestimated the constraints. In the particular case of strings, the improvement is driven by the $B$-mode data, and is especially pronounced for Abelian-Higgs strings. We also present forecasts for the Simons Observatory and the LiteBIRD satellite: the former will improve string tension constraints by about a factor of three, while the latter those on the domain wall tension by about a factor of five. Finally, we assess the impact of Nambu-Goto string loops on CMB anisotropies in light of both current and future observations.

[L85] We investigate signatures of chirality at Chern insulator transitions in the presence of a boundary. The transition between a trivial insulator and a Chern insulator with Chern number $C=1$ is described by a massless Dirac fermion whose parity anomaly gives a critical Hall conductivity $σ_{xy}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{h}$. Using a Dirac mass domain wall construction, we show that the chiral edge mode delocalizes into the bulk at criticality, but the boundary fermion correlation function retains a chiral structure and acquires the scaling dimension of the bulk fermion. We compute current correlation functions and demonstrate that the anomaly of the bulk Hall response is matched by delocalized chiral modes near the boundary. Using only the residual conformal symmetry of a (2+1)d conformal field theory (CFT) in a half-space, we identify parity-odd terms in current and energy-momentum tensor correlation functions that encode these modes and determine their electromagnetic and gravitational anomaly coefficients. Our analysis therefore applies to general time-reversal breaking (2+1)d CFTs, beyond the free Dirac transition. In particular, the analysis of the gravitational anomaly is also applicable to the free Majorana CFT governing the transition between a trivial superconductor and a topological superconductor. We also extend our results to more general Chern number changing transitions and to the transition between a (3+1)d topological insulator and a trivial insulator.

[L99] In this paper, we employ the soft ellipsoid contact type potential (ECP) in a generic coarse grained model of DNA and study the renaturation process. The interactions between the bases are modeled using our ECP type potential, along with other interactions to capture bending, dihedral and solvent effects implicitly. Structure and helix formation is primarily driven by non-spherical geometry of the bases and excluded volume effects. Simulation results demonstrate that two isolated strands in a random initial configuration undergo spontaneous helix formation during annealing. The model captures the qualitative features of the coil-helix transition as well as the morphology of the helical structure. However, the present parameterization of our model does not yet capture the proper right chirality and detailed helical geometry associated with DNA. Thus, its capability for making any quantitative predictions remains limited. Statistical and physical properties of our model are discussed in detail.

[L113] The Expanding Box Model (EBM) has been widely employed to simulate multiscale plasma phenomena in the expanding solar wind by transforming the MHD equations to a co-moving, non-inertial frame. However, traditional formulations have suffered from historical ambiguity regarding the physical separation between the co-moving and inertial reference frames, primarily arising from a classical approximation of an invariant magnetic field between them. To resolve this inconsistency, we reformulate the EBM from first principles using a fully covariant approach. Here, we model the expanding solar wind frame as an anisotropic expanding spacetime metric, allowing us to incorporate radial acceleration profiles and differential transverse expansion, ensuring that all physical fields are correctly transformed by expansion. We demonstrate that asymmetries identified in previous EBM-MHD literature are direct consequences of neglecting the tensorial scaling of the magnetic field. Our covariant treatment eliminates these residues, restoring symmetry in the co-moving frame. Projecting our system back into the inertial frame clarifies the distinction between local plasma dynamics and plasma expansion, revealing the anisotropy of the Parker spiral as a geometric projection. Furthermore, linear wave analysis using Elsässer variables reveals that plasma expansion induces a low-frequency cutoff and geometric damping. Numerical integration demonstrates that expansion drives the reflection of Alfvén waves, generating counter-propagating modes primarily at low frequencies relative to the expansion rate, while high frequencies converge to the WKB approximation. This provides a consistent foundation for simulations, establishing that expansion can serve as a source of counter-propagating waves necessary to drive solar wind turbulence at low frequencies.

parts: The v0.7 changes are doing useful cleanup. Several previous “top” hits have dropped sharply once biology/CFT/math-context controls and tighter bundles were added, while the curved-waveguide paper rises as a genuinely integrated case. That is exactly the direction we wanted: fewer surface matches, more weight on connected mechanism.

Yes — this batch is more useful than the first one, but for a slightly different purpose.

The key change is that v0.7 is scanning by **last-updated date**, not just first submission date. It fetched 2,121 records updated during September 1–8, 2026; 252 had primary categories outside the requested set, and the reporting layer now keeps track of that explicitly. fileciteturn260file1L45-L55 That means this is best interpreted as a **current research-activity/revival snapshot**: an older paper revised now counts as activity now, while its original claim date remains its original publication date.

I ran the full `all_scored` table rather than looking only at the eight reported hits. Among the 1,869 papers whose primary category is actually in scope:

- 245, or **13.1%**, activated at least one positive feature.
- 39, or **2.09%**, activated at least two.
- 8, or **0.43%**, activated at least three.
- Exactly **one paper, 0.054%**, activated four.
- Only **three papers, 0.16%**, triggered one of the 23 compound bundles.

That is an important calibration result. The current literature contains plenty of individual old ingredients, but **integrated conjunctions remain extremely rare**. That is exactly the distinction our Bayesian test needs.

The new scanner also looks substantially less gullible. On papers shared with v0.4:

- “Eye-opening bounds on cusps” fell **13.35 → 9.20**.
- The Cartan–Hadamard topology paper fell **12.00 → 8.15**.
- The deconfined-criticality line-defect paper fell **11.29 → 2.99**.
- The `N`-bein paper remained relatively high, **11.20 → 10.50**.
- The cell-biology topology hit still scores highly structurally, but is now correctly excluded from the primary-category report rather than masquerading as physics evidence.

So the controls/filtering are beginning to separate “shares vocabulary/geometry” from “belongs in our actual test.”

The standout new object is very clearly **“Torsion-induced gauge structure in curved quantum waveguides.”** It was first posted June 2, 2026 and revised September 2. The abstract gives an unusually tight chain:

**particle confined near a space curve → finite transverse width → projection onto transverse modes → Frenet normal-frame rotation → gauge potential determined by curve torsion → closed-curve holonomy from integrated torsion → geometric interference → same mechanism reproduced in a classical elastic rod.** fileciteturn260file1L186-L234

That is exactly the kind of paper our prior says deserves attention. Not because “torsion,” “holonomy,” or “elastic rod” are novel—they emphatically aren't—but because several old constructions are being made to do **one connected job**, with geometry generating something normally written as gauge structure.

I would not yet call it anomalous. Its correct status is:

**high-priority 2024-baseline probe.**

The question is now very specific: how normal was that conjunction by the end of 2024? Curved quantum waveguides, Frenet frames, torsion, Berry/Wilczek–Zee connections and elastic rods all have antecedents. What matters is whether **finite-width curve geometry → normal-frame torsion → induced gauge potential → holonomy → classical continuum analogue** was already an active package or whether these pieces were still largely compartmentalized.

The `N`-bein paper is the second interesting one. It takes Cartan-frame language into quantum parameter space, combines a Wilczek–Zee connection with a torsion-like tensor, and constructs gauge-invariant observables from that geometry. fileciteturn260file2L129-L155 Again, the interesting question is not whether differential geometry existed. It is whether this **migration of old frame/connection/torsion machinery into foundational quantum-state geometry** was common in 2024.

The pre-geometric gravity paper is more mixed. It explicitly makes effective metric and classical gravity emerge and reunifies curvature, torsion and nonmetricity. fileciteturn260file2L115-L127 That's relevant to the revival/convergence measurement, but I would give it substantially less SAT-likeness than the raw scanner does because it uses a Yang–Mills gauge construction plus a Higgs-like field and spontaneous symmetry breaking. It moves toward emergence but not obviously toward SAT's **austerity/reduction of primitives**.

Most of the rest are good controls:

Cosmic strings/domain walls: old, active native lineage.  
Chern boundary chirality: native condensed matter.  
DNA chirality/coarse-graining: native biology/material geometry.  
Line defects at criticality: native defect/CFT machinery.  
Foliation/contact-geometry papers: useful synonym controls but not physics convergence.

There's another interesting numerical wrinkle. Of the 1,869 in-scope papers:

- 1,157 were genuinely new submissions during this week.
- 712 were older papers being revised.
- Positive-feature incidence was **11.5% among new submissions versus 15.7% among revisions**.
- Three-or-more-feature conjunctions were **0.26% among new papers versus 0.70% among revisions**.

I would not interpret that yet as “revival.” Revised papers naturally differ from new submissions in lots of ways. But it is exactly why keeping the update stream is useful: if old geometric/classical papers are disproportionately receiving renewed development in 2025–26, that becomes independently measurable.

So this batch strengthens the design more than it strengthens any causal hypothesis. I would make essentially **no major posterior shift yet**.

What it does tell us is that our crucial statistic is going to work:

> **2024 frequency of integrated bundles versus 2025–26 frequency of those same bundles, with native-domain and cross-domain migration separated.**

And v0.7 has uncovered a very good test case for that: the torsion/curve/gauge/holonomy paper. If 2024 is full of those, it gets zero surprise. If 2024 has all five ingredients but almost never connected that way, while 2025–26 starts producing several such integrations, that's exactly the signal we defined before seeing this result.
The way to isolate hypotheses is to narrow by date window and coss reference by similar feature and the first SAT public discussion of that feature.

Exactly. That is cleaner than comparing “2024” to “2026” wholesale.

The natural unit is not the year. It is the **feature-specific exposure event**.

For every SAT/H(s)H feature \(F_i\), define:

\[
T_{0,i}=\text{first independently verifiable public SAT discussion of }F_i
\]

Usually that should be the podcast, because the archive often records things months after they were discussed publicly.

Then build the outside-literature timeline around that \(T_0\).

The basic event-study windows I’d use are:

- **Deep baseline:** Jan. 2022 → Dec. 2023
- **Immediate baseline:** Jan. 2024 → \(T_0-1\)
- **Very-early post:** \(T_0\) → \(T_0+3\) months
- **Early post:** \(T_0+3\) → \(T_0+9\) months
- **Later post:** \(T_0+9\) → \(T_0+18\) months
- **Current:** thereafter

And we do that separately for every feature or compound claim.

That lets us distinguish several hypotheses much more sharply.

If a feature is already rising strongly **before** \(T_0\), that supports ordinary independent field development.

If it is flat or niche before \(T_0\), then rises after \(T_0\), that is evidence against a simple “2024 continuation” model—but not yet evidence of transmission.

If the rise occurs after \(T_0\) with a plausible research lag, especially in fields adjacent to the likely exposure pathway, that increases the likelihood of diffusion.

If several different features rise after their **own individual SAT discussion dates**, rather than all rising together because of one general zeitgeist shift, that becomes much more diagnostic.

That last point is probably the strongest test available.

Suppose SAT discusses:

**A** in February 2025,  
**B** in May 2025,  
**C** in January 2026,  
**D** in March 2026.

The diffusion hypothesis predicts something closer to:

\[
A \rightarrow \text{outside rise first}
\]

then

\[
B \rightarrow \text{outside rise}
\]

then \(C\), then \(D\),

with appropriate lags.

A generic “physics was moving this way anyway” hypothesis has much less reason to reproduce the **ordering of SAT's public feature sequence**.

So I would actually make **sequence correspondence** one of our primary Bayesian observables.

For each feature:

\[
E_i(\tau)=
\frac{r_i(T_{0,i}+\tau)}
{r_i(\text{2024 baseline})}
\]

where \(r_i\) is normalized arXiv prevalence.

Then compare features after shifting each one so its public SAT exposure sits at \(\tau=0\).

That produces an **exposure-aligned event curve**.

If there is no transmission-related effect, aligning unrelated research topics on SAT's podcast dates should not magically produce a common post-zero increase.

If there is some causal contribution, we might see something like:

\[
E(\tau<0)\approx1
\]

followed by

\[
E(\tau>0)>1
\]

with a peak several months later.

And we should do the same thing for the **compound relations**, not only individual vocabulary. Your synonymy file is particularly useful here because it lets us recognize a claim after disciplinary translation—for example projection/readout as dimensional reduction, quotienting or hypersurface restriction; connection as parallel transport; particle-as-cut as dimensional/hypersurface intersection. fileciteturn258file2L149-L193

The strongest hierarchy would therefore be:

**Level 1 — feature prevalence**

Did torsion, holonomy, worldtubes, framed curves, nonorientability, structured vacuum, etc. increase?

Weak evidence by itself.

**Level 2 — domain migration**

Did something formerly concentrated in differential geometry, condensed matter, fluid mechanics, or analogue models start appearing as an actual particle/gravity/cosmology mechanism?

Much stronger.

**Level 3 — compound architecture**

Did things like:

curve → torsion → gauge structure → holonomy

or

persistent extended history → slicing/projection → local particle property

or

topology → chirality/CP → baryogenesis

begin appearing?

Much stronger still.

**Level 4 — exposure-order correspondence**

Did those different compound structures begin appearing externally in roughly the order in which their SAT analogues became public?

This is where the hypotheses really separate.

And there is another very useful control.

For every exposed SAT feature \(F_i\), choose one or more **neighbor features that SAT had not yet publicly discussed at \(T_{0,i}\)** but which belong to similar literatures.

Then ask whether both rise.

If both rise equally, ordinary field dynamics is a good explanation.

If the publicly exposed feature rises while otherwise comparable not-yet-exposed SAT features do not—and later those other features rise after *their* own public dates—that would be far harder to explain as simple trend selection.

So our dataset wants columns something like:

| Feature | SAT first-public date | 2024 baseline rate | Pre-\(T_0\) slope | 0–3m | 3–9m | 9–18m | Domains before | Domains after | Compound partners | Sequence rank |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---:|

Then a separate causal table:

| Observation | H0: ordinary continuation | H1: independent convergence | H2: DAI/RMS-mediated diffusion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Already rising before SAT | high | high | neutral/negative |
| Rise only after SAT | moderate | moderate | higher |
| 2–9 month lag | neutral | neutral | higher |
| Migration from old niche | moderate | high | high |
| Multiple old ideas integrate | low | moderate | high |
| Rise follows SAT feature sequence | very low | low | high |
| Unexposed controls rise identically | high | high | negative |
| Lexical similarity disappears but structural relation survives | neutral | high | high |
| Network follows AI/philosophy → foundations → physics | low | moderate | high |

And importantly, the scanner we now have can support this because it already distinguishes individual features from compound bundles and records the raw corpus denominator. The current v0.7 run has 102 features and 23 bundles, so we can use the same frozen translation grammar across historical windows rather than inventing searches after seeing results. fileciteturn260file1L48-L55

So yes: I think the next job is not another generalized SAT-likeness scan.

It is to build the **feature → first-public-SAT-date ledger**, and then query narrow external windows around each one.

That should give us a much cleaner Bayesian experiment.
Ok, we've got tons of timelines in the archive. And don't you already have one built in this thread?

Yes. We already built one in this thread, and I should use it instead of acting like we need to start over.

The timeline already assembled here includes the major claim/public-exposure anchors:

- pre-public SAT/RMS formation through 2024
- February 2, 2025: first public DAI/RMS/SAT launch and filament-unification discussion
- February–April 2025: AI/consciousness/RMS/philosophy-of-science bridge period
- May 8, 2025: several locked prediction sets
- June–November 2025: continued RMS/AI/philosophy plus increasingly formal SAT
- December 24–28, 2025: physics/archive-release cluster
- January 2026: 0.24-rad/Hubble/dark-matter/predictions cluster
- February–March 2026: open-source TOE/formalization ramp
- March 7, 2026: scalar-angular torsion / 4D superhelical unification public transcript
- March 16, 2026: neutrino/photon, timesheet/intersection, θ₄/mass public material
- March–April 2026: Bell/Minkowski/foundations and AI/LLM-adjacent bridge material
- May 2026: electrogravity, boson reclassification, conservative-methodology, predictions, black-hole/unification material
- June 2026 onward: explicit 2024-vs-2026/paradigm-comparison phase

And before that, from the uploaded conversation, we had already recovered a more specific **ranking chronology**: 2024 as the control bed; Feb. 2025 as the first public threshold; spring–May 2025 as the tight early comparison window; Dec. 2025 as the full-archive exposure threshold; 2026 as the broader proliferation/convergence period.

So the efficient move now is not “build a feature-date ledger from scratch.” It is:

**Take the timeline we already have + the archive timelines + the podcast transcripts, and annotate each SAT/H(s)H feature with the earliest public discussion date.**

Then for each feature we run the external literature windows around that date.

In other words, the timeline already exists. What we need now is just the **feature-indexed version of it**.

I was unnecessarily re-deriving infrastructure we already have.
Ok, lets break tose down more granularly, particularly the earlier ones, which startt with the Fundamental INtuitions, basically the 5 Feb 25 episode of DAI

Yes. I’ll make February 5, 2025 the real starting line and decompose the early period episode-by-episode/claim-by-claim, using “Fundamental Intuitions” as the anchor rather than the looser February 2 launch material.

######################
FAIR WARNING

######################
THE MATERIALS CONTAINED HEREIN ARE ROUGHLY SORTED, ROUGHLY WRITTEN, AND... NOT ROUGHLY THOUGHT THROUGH, BUT MORE "ROUGH-AND-READILY THOUGHT THROUGH" Direct any questions to Nathan McKnight (nathanmcknight@gmail.com)
INTRODUCTION TO THE INDEX

This is basically a personal archive and indexing system for my own use, so that I can access my files more conveniently. That said, it's also an idea that anybody is welcome to consider, share, and work with. Started very small, and only grew because once the original ontological commitments were established, so many other things fell into place. Naturally, intuitively. If you decide to make use of this material, feel free to strike up a conversation. It's been a lot to work on for a long time, and it's about time it had a public face. This is the start.
SAT - Scalar-Angular-Torsion Theory
The FUNDAMENTAL INTUITIONS of SAT
0th: The "real world" is the world of particle worldlines plotted in four dimensions; it is a hypercomplex tangled "Zottenwelt" of worldlines--SAT calls these worldlines filaments (to distinguish from strings in String Theory proper).
1st: Time moves like a wavefront through these worldlines--SAT calls this wavefront the time surface.
2nd: What we perceive as a fundamental particle is the intersection of the particle's worldline with the time wavefront.
PILLAR NUMBER ONE: The Standard Model of Particle Physics is the evolving three-dimensional structure of everything--from quarks to organisms to the entire observable universe, and probably beyond. The organizational structure of the universe can be viewed as braided threads, tangled yarns, thick ropes, and ultimately a vast complex and highly structured literal fabric of reality, and envisioning these structures and their interactions in four dimensions (or scaled down to three) may give useful intuitive insights into actual physical phenomena.
PROPOSITION A: Unless forced to do otherwise by evidence or the internal logic of SAT, the theory will treat the entirety of the Standard Model of Particle Physics as essentially accurate, and will consider it fully imported into the theory with little or no change, apart from conceptual translation into the geometry of SAT.
3rd: There must be a real interaction between the time wavefront and these worldlines--a transfer of energy from the wavefront to the worldlines, vice versa, or (most likely), both.
4th: These interactions govern particle formation and stability.
5th: These interactions must exert a force back on the wavefront as well.
6th: This back-transmission of energy from the filament network (Zottenwelt) creates curvature of the time surface.

I checked it. Your memory is close, but I would not use **February 5, 2025** as the exact publication date.

The archive supports a very tight **February 2–4, 2025 initial public SAT burst**:

- **Feb. 2:** *What Is Thought Made Of? [Filament Unification Intro]* — first unmistakable public filament/SAT introduction. fileciteturn266file0L2-L2
- **Feb. 3:** *Stringing Ourselves Along* — explicitly described as a “toy theory” taking the four-dimensional structure of spacetime seriously. fileciteturn272file0L2-L2
- **Feb. 4:** a much denser SAT/4D cluster: *Thought and the Structure of Spacetime*, *The Cosmic Loom*, *The 4-Dimensional Structure of Thought*, and the two 4D Biology episodes. fileciteturn272file0L2-L2

I don't see a podcast release on **Feb. 5** in the cleaned episode chronology. There was audience activity that day—the engagement data shows five audience events/segments on Feb. 5—which may be part of why that date is familiar. fileciteturn270file5L81-L92

The actual *Fundamental Intuitions* document is clearly the right conceptual baseline. It already contains essentially the entire primitive early SAT grammar: persistent 4D worldlines/filaments; moving time surface; particles as intersections; braided hierarchical structure; reciprocal filament/time-surface interaction; emergent GR curvature; constrained future/past force propagation; particle properties from intersection geometry; θ₄/mass; helical intersection traces; geometric QCD/spin/flavor; constants from geometry; bosons as transmitted/ripple phenomena; aligned vacuum filaments; and matter/vacuum as different configurations of the same underlying structure. fileciteturn265file0L2-L2

So for our Bayesian chronology I would mark the opening epoch as:

**T₀ = February 2–4, 2025 — Fundamental-Intuitions public-release cluster**

and then assign **feature-specific \(T_0\)** inside those three days wherever we can determine the earliest episode.

That is actually better than forcing everything onto one date. For example:

| Earliest public window | Claim family |
|---|---|
| **Feb. 2** | filament/worldline ontology; 4D physical structure; particle/intersection picture; early RMS/SAT bridge |
| **Feb. 3** | explicit “take 4D spacetime literally” / Stringing Along framing |
| **Feb. 4** | tapestry/loom/bundling; extended 4D information/thought structure; richer cross-scale elaboration |

And I would treat **Feb. 5 only as a convenient approximate marker**, not a provenance date.

This also means our first external comparison window can be extremely tight: **pre-Feb. 2, Feb. 2–4, then post-Feb. 4**, rather than just “before/after February 2025.”
